questions.title: What is exponential gating in xLSTM and why replace sigmoid gates?
questions.question_body: I am reading Section~2 where the authors define i[t] = \exp(pre_i[t]) instead of using a sigmoid activation function sigma(.). The paper says exponential gates allow larger dynamic range and help revise stored information, but I am confused about two things: (1) What specific limitation of sigmoid gates motivates switching to an exponential form? (2) Since an exponential can grow very large very quickly, how do the authors prevent overflow or numerical instability when training large models? The text mentions a stabiliser state m[t], but I do not see clearly how it interacts with i[t] and f[t].

questions.title: How does the normaliser state n[t] work in scalar sLSTM and matrix mLSTM?
questions.question_body: Equations~(6)-(9) introduce an extra accumulator called n[t]. For sLSTM it follows n[t] = f[t]*n[t-1] + i[t]; for mLSTM it becomes n[t] = f[t]*n[t-1] + i[t]*k[t]. I am trying to understand its purpose: Why do we need this extra term when computing h[t]? How exactly is n[t] used as denominator when forming h[t] (= c[t]/n[t] for sLSTM or C[t]*q[t]/max(|n[t]^T q[t]|,1) for mLSTM)? What would happen if we omitted n[t] altogether?
